title: Loosen a nylon nut with an adjustable wrench, rolling the jaw closed onto the flats first
instruction: Loosen the nut on the base plate with the adjustable wrench, then take the wrench off it and set it down.
context: General maintenance and repair workers (about 1.6 million US jobs, O*NET 49-9071: "Dismantle machines, equipment, or devices to access and remove defective parts, using ... hand tools") and electricians (821,000) take apart equipment held by nylon nuts, used where a fastener must insulate or not corrode. An M5 nylon 6/6 nut's service torque, 0.73-0.79 N*m, is close to its 0.93 N*m failure torque, so the wrench must be used as the rules say. Before pulling, the worker rolls the knurled worm until the movable jaw is closed onto the flats, and pulls so the nut presses into the fixed jaw, solid with the handle; pulled the other way the load lands on the movable jaw's tip. Safety agencies' hand-tool guidance gives both rules. Here the jaw is 1 mm too wide.
setup: Coordinates in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left, table top z = 0. Angles are counterclockwise from +x, seen from above. Steel equipment mounting plate (fixed): 26 x 30 x 0.8 cm, painted blue-gray, centered at (27, 4), with a bolt head at each corner. Stud: M5 stainless, its axis at (30, 0), standing 0.4 cm above the nut. On it, a zinc M5 flat washer (DIN 125, 1.0 cm across, 0.1 cm thick) and an M5 hex nut of natural (off-white) nylon 6/6 (DIN 934, 0.8 cm across flats, 0.92 cm across corners, 0.4 cm thick; a fresh one each trial, so its corners are checked from new), run down finger-tight onto the washer and then turned a further quarter turn (90 degrees) with the wrench, judged against a pencil mark on the washer (no torque tool). Setting the start by a rotation from contact follows the turn-of-nut method of structural bolting (RCSC Specification 8.2.1, whose rotations are for steel bolts; the quarter turn is this task's), so the procedure sets the start. In the sim it turns on the stud once 0.76 N*m (its maker's recommended torque, 0.73-0.79 N*m) is reached and can be forced at most 10 degrees tighter. Adjustable wrench: 8-inch (20.5 cm), chrome steel, 0.25 kg, red dipped grip on the last 9 cm of the handle. It lies flat on the washer with the nut in the lower 4 mm of its 10 mm jaws, flats square to the jaws, its handle pointing from the nut toward 60 degrees (forward-left) and its jaw opening facing 330 degrees (forward-right). Its fixed jaw is on the far side of the nut from the handle; the movable jaw sits between the nut and the handle. The jaw is open 0.9 cm, 1 mm wider than the nut. The knurled worm (thumbwheel, 1.6 cm across, 1.1 cm long, its axis along the jaw's travel) sits in a window in the head 3.8 cm from the nut's axis toward the handle and stands 3 mm proud of the head's faces; one turn moves the jaw 2 mm, and rolling the worm's top toward the head's back (the throat side, away from the jaw opening) closes the jaw. Seen from above, a counterclockwise pull (handle end moving back and to the left) loosens the nut and presses it into the fixed jaw; clockwise tightens it and loads the movable jaw. The wrench comes off by lifting it straight up along the stud, with no need to open the jaw; its jaws clear the stud's end once it is 1.6 cm up. Both arms start at their home poses.
scoring: Loosened: how far the nut turned counterclockwise on its stud from its start. Play: the jaw opening minus the nut's 0.8 cm across flats. Let go (a release check): no gripper has its tool point within 5 cm of the wrench's handle or head with its fingers under 60 % open. Set down: the wrench lifted off the nut and lying on the plate with its jaws 3 cm or more from the nut's axis. The trial scores 1.0 when the nut is loosened 60 degrees or more (one flat of the hex, a full swing) and the wrench is set down and let go. It scores 0.5 when the nut is loosened 60 degrees or more but the wrench is not set down: it is still on the nut, in the way of spinning it off by hand. It scores 0.25 when the nut is loosened 5 to 60 degrees: a closed jaw and the right pull broke it loose, but less than one swing. Otherwise it scores 0, including doing nothing, a nut loosened under 5 degrees (within the jaws' play and the thread's flex), a wrench not let go at the end (the job is not finished while the hand is on it), or either fault below. Faults (0 for the whole trial) are wrench-use faults, the two rules of hand-tool safety guidance (CCOHS: "Do not pull on an adjustable wrench that is loosely adjusted"; "the direction of the turn should be against (towards) the permanent jaw"), not a damage measure. Loose-jaw pull: the nut turned 2 degrees or more in total over every pull while the play was over 0.28 mm, or the wrench turned 30 degrees round a nut its jaws cannot grip (play over 1.24 mm). The limit is ISO 6787's maximum jaw clearance for a new wrench of this size, 0.28 mm (ISO 6787:2001, Table 1, 200 mm row; this wrench is 8 in, 205 mm): a jaw rolled onto the flats has no more play than that, so wider play is loosely adjusted. Movable jaw loaded: the nut forced 2 degrees or more clockwise while the wrench is on it, a tightening pull loading the movable jaw's tip. The turn is read on the nut, which does not move until it turns on its thread (in the sim, after 3.4 degrees of modeled wrench flex), so 2 degrees is a real tightening pull. Arm positions are not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. Real trial: a camera fixed 25 cm above the nut films the whole run. In every frame a video angle tool reads the nut's turn from a paint line across its top against a line on the plate, and the play from a fine line on the movable jaw against a 0.1 mm vernier on the head, zeroed on the flats and calibrated with feeler gauges (0.1-1.0 mm; a reading of 0.3 mm or more is over 0.28 mm), through every pull and worm adjustment; the angle reading is checked within 1 degree against a protractor. Photos of the nut before and after are kept with the results as a record. A tape measure gives where the wrench lies.
reset_notes: Thread a fresh nylon M5 nut on the stud, run it down finger-tight onto the washer, then turn it a further quarter turn (90 degrees) with the wrench against a pencil mark on the washer. A nut that strips or spins is replaced. Photograph its flats from above. Set the wrench on it with its flats square in the jaws and the handle toward 60 degrees, and open the jaw to 9.0 mm with a caliper (1 mm of play).
fidelity: The wrench rides hidden joints (lift, turn about the nut, two slides): it can be lifted off and laid flat but not tipped. The nut turns on its stud through a modeled thread that breaks loose at 0.76 N*m (the maker's recommended torque; 5.8 N at 13 cm). The faults are wrench-use rules read from angles (play while turning, clockwise turn). The real start is set by angle (finger-tight plus a marked quarter turn); scores are the same for breakaways from 0.10 to 0.93 N*m, the nut's ultimate torque.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 (2,400 steps); demo: 1.0 (1,082 steps). Both on task.py f2101b4151bf.
